links.note: Johann Wilhelm Petersen, later a leading radical Pietist, often went to the prayer meeting in Spener's house. There he heard talk of the church's future. Alexander Mack, who founded the Brethren in 1708, wrote that they had once lived 'among the pietists'. A Brethren historian wrote in 1899 that Francke woke Ernst Christoph Hochmann to faith at Halle, and that Hochmann shaped Mack more than anyone. links.note: In 1785 Wesley wrote that he had varied from the Church of England's discipline, though not from its doctrines, and only 'by constraint'. sources.quote: We received yesterday from the hands of the Secre- tary of Propaganda the worthy present, so welcomed by Us, of the Armenian Bible, and We return you heartfelt thanks .

sources.work: Malachia Ormanian, The Church of Armenia, tr. G. Marcar Gregory (London, 1912)
sources.locus: ch. on the eighteenth century, pp. 86-87
sources.quote: Accordingly he gave his sanction to the establishment of an Armeho- Catholic patriarchate which was officially subject to the Roman Curia (1742).

sources.work: Minas Nurikhan, The Life and Times of Abbot Mechitar, tr. John McQuillan (Venice, 1915)
sources.quote: This Catholic movement gave rise to the . insti- tution of the Armenian-Catholic Patriarchate of Ci- licia by the Sovereign Pontiff, Benedict XIV, in 1742, with many privileges.

prose_changes.old: Pietism grew out of Lutheran devotion together with the influence of Dutch Reformed precisianism, and gave rise in turn to the Moravian Church and the wider Protestant missionary movement. Württemberg Pietism, associated with Johann Albrecht Bengel, belongs within this same movement.
prose_changes.new: Pietism grew out of Lutheran devotion. Spener's Pia Desideria first came out as a preface to a book of sermons by Johann Arndt. Pietism may also owe something to the strict Dutch Reformed piety called precisianism, but how much is not clear. Pietism shaped the Moravian Church at Herrnhut. It also sent some of the first Protestant missions out of Europe. Pietism in Württemberg, linked with Johann Albrecht Bengel, belongs to this same movement.
prose_changes.reason: 'Gave rise in turn to the Moravian Church' overstates: the Herrnhut refugees came from the old Unity, and Pietism reached them through Zinzendorf (now the influenced link). 'The influence of Dutch Reformed precisianism' is stated as fact, but no vendored Pietist text names a Dutch source, so it is qualified with the reason. 'Gave rise to the wider Protestant missionary movement' becomes 'sent some of the first Protestant missions out of Europe', the entry's own claim and supported by Guericke on Tranquebar. The Lutheran root is kept and now shown: Pia Desideria began as a preface to Arndt's postil. Old field scored FRE 27; whole field rewritten. Round 1: R1-23: 'no early Pietist text we hold names a Dutch source' was build language; now states the uncertainty plainly. Long sentence split.

prose_changes.old: Pietism never became a denomination of its own — it stayed inside the Lutheran churches and eventually dissolved as a distinct party — but almost everything it touched outlived it. The Moravians at Herrnhut came out of its orbit and through them John Wesley; the Protestant missionary movement's first sustained institutional base was at Halle. And the Halle foundations themselves are still standing and still working in Saxony-Anhalt, orphanage buildings, library, cabinet of curiosities and all. Its habits — small groups meeting midweek to read Scripture, and the expectation that a Christian can tell the story of their own conversion — are now so ordinary across evangelical Protestantism that their origin is easy to miss.
prose_changes.new: Pietism never became a church of its own. It stayed inside the Lutheran churches and in time faded as a separate party. But almost everything it touched outlived it. The Moravians at Herrnhut grew up close to it. Their patron, Count Zinzendorf, was Spener's godson and went to school at Halle. John Wesley learned from the Moravians, and in 1738 he went to Halle himself. George Whitefield took Francke's orphan house as the model for his own in Georgia. Halle also chose and backed the first missionaries the king of Denmark sent to India, in 1706. The Halle foundations still stand and still work in Saxony-Anhalt: the orphanage buildings, the library, the cabinet of curiosities and all. Its habits are now so ordinary across evangelical Protestantism that their origin is easy to miss. Small groups meet midweek to read Scripture. A Christian is expected to tell the story of their own conversion.
prose_changes.reason: 'Through them John Wesley' is replaced by what the sources show: Wesley learned from the Moravians and also went to Halle himself in 1738; Whitefield modeled his Georgia orphan house on Francke's (both in the new influenced link). The unsupported superlative 'the Protestant missionary movement's first sustained institutional base was at Halle' becomes Halle's documented role in choosing and backing the 1706 Danish mission (Guericke). Zinzendorf's Spener and Halle ties are added to carry the Moravian link. Every other fact kept; the old field scored FRE 27 and FK 16.5, so it is rewritten whole in shorter sentences.

prose_changes.old: Between Pietism and Anabaptism - a real uniqueness test
prose_changes.new: Radical Pietism grew out of German Pietism, among people who left the state churches. Out of it came the Brethren. They joined Pietist inward faith to Anabaptist ways: baptism for believers only, plain living and refusal of the sword.
prose_changes.reason: The old text, 'a real uniqueness test', is internal build language, not public prose. Rewritten as the two relationships the entry names: descent from German Pietism and the taking up of Anabaptist ways, both now linked.

prose_changes.old: Radical child of the Puritan ferment; parent-influence on abolition
prose_changes.new: The Quakers grew out of the most radical wing of the Puritan upheaval in England. Many of the first Friends came from Independent and Baptist churches. Later, their campaigning did much to end slavery.
prose_changes.reason: 'Radical child of the Puritan ferment; parent-influence on abolition' is note-form, and 'parent-influence' is jargon. Rewritten in full sentences. The abolition claim is kept in plain words; the London Yearly Meeting epistles from the 1750s on carry the Society's campaign against the slave trade, and abolition has no entry to link to.

prose_changes.old: This community is a direct renewal of the old Bohemian Unity of the Brethren, carried across the hidden century between its suppression in 1627 and the refugees' arrival at Herrnhut in 1722. Its episcopal succession was renewed through the Jablonski-Nitschmann consecration of 1735, tying it formally back to the old Unity. It had a decisive influence on John Wesley, and began sending missionaries decades before any other Protestant body did.
prose_changes.new: This community saw itself as the old Bohemian Unity of the Brethren made new. In its own telling, the Unity was suppressed in 1627 and survived in hiding for a century. Then its refugees reached Herrnhut in 1722. In 1735 the old Unity's senior bishop, Daniel Ernst Jablonski, made David Nitschmann a bishop. That tied the new church formally to the old one. Yet its patron, Count Zinzendorf, was a Lutheran Pietist. At first he meant Herrnhut as a gathering inside the Lutheran church. It had a deep effect on John Wesley. From 1732 it sent missionaries far overseas.
prose_changes.reason: 'A direct renewal of the old Bohemian Unity' presents the community's own reading as settled; the continued-as link is Contested, since Zinzendorf first meant Herrnhut as a Lutheran Pietist gathering (Spangenberg). Now framed as the community's own view, with the other side stated. 'Began sending missionaries decades before any other Protestant body did' is wrong: Halle's Danish mission reached Tranquebar in 1706 (the Pietism entry's own text; Guericke), 26 years before 1732. Now 'from 1732 it sent missionaries far overseas'. The Jablonski-Nitschmann consecration is kept and spelled out from Cranz. Old field scored FRE 27; rewritten whole.

prose_changes.old: The Moravian Church is a living worldwide body, and far larger outside Europe than in it. The great majority of its members are in Tanzania and the Caribbean, the long fruit of the mission work begun in 1732. Its most consequential single contact was with a young Anglican priest: John Wesley met Moravians in a storm at sea and again in London, and the Methodist revival carries their fingerprints. The Losungen, a book of daily Scripture texts drawn by lot at Herrnhut and printed every year since 1731, is still published and read in dozens of languages. One of the longest unbroken publishing runs in the world. And the hidden-seed story ended well: a church suppressed in Bohemia in 1627 has descendants in every continent.
prose_changes.new: The Moravian Church is a living worldwide body, and far larger outside Europe than in it. Most of its members are in Tanzania and the Caribbean, the long fruit of the mission work begun in 1732. Its most important single contact was with a young Anglican priest. John Wesley met Moravians in a storm at sea and again in London, and the Methodist revival carries their fingerprints. The Losungen is a book of daily Bible texts, drawn by lot at Herrnhut and printed every year since 1731. prose_changes.old: The awakening grew out of New England Puritanism and became a parent of later American revival culture and the missionary movement. It also reached into the middle and southern colonies, through preachers like the Tennents and the revival at Hanover, Virginia — though historians are divided on whether that counts as part of the same movement or a separate one. Through the Black and Native Christian writing it produced, it stands among the parent traditions of the Black Church in America.
prose_changes.new: The awakening grew out of New England's Puritan churches. Jonathan Edwards built on their books. George Whitefield, the English Methodist preacher, made it normal to preach from town to town. It also reached the middle and southern colonies, through preachers like the Tennents and the revival at Hanover, Virginia. Historians do not agree whether that was the same movement or another one. William Carey, who began the Baptist mission to India, held up its missionary David Brainerd as a model. Later American revivals and the Black Church may owe it a debt too. How direct that debt was is hard to say.
prose_changes.reason: Three claims corrected. 'Parent of later American revival culture' and 'among the parent traditions of the Black Church' have no vendored support and are now said plainly as possibilities. 'Parent of the missionary movement' is made concrete (Carey and Brainerd, documented). Whitefield's role (documented through Chauncy) is added because the text's own description names it. Puritan descent is kept as 'grew out of New England's Puritan churches'. The Tennents and Hanover sentence and its open question are kept. Rewritten whole for reading level. Round 1: R1-23: build language removed; the debt stays qualified. Round 2 (R2-01): last sentence replaced with the reviewer's wording, which states the uncertainty without a claim about what scholars have or have not traced.

prose_changes.old: It began in the winter of 1734-35 in Northampton, Massachusetts, where the town's minister, Jonathan Edwards, watched an ordinary Connecticut Valley congregation come apart and remake itself in a wave of conversions. And then did something unusual: he wrote down what had happened, case by case, including a young woman the town had thought beyond hope and a four-year-old girl. When the English preacher George Whitefield toured the colonies from 1739, scattered local revivals became a general one, with itinerants crossing parish lines and crowds gathering in the open air. It split New England's churches: the New Lights defended the awakening, the Old Lights — Charles Chauncy of Boston foremost among them — attacked it as enthusiasm and disorder, and hundreds of Separate congregations broke away, a great many of them becoming Baptist. It also produced the first substantial body of Christian writing by Black and Native people in the colonies.
prose_changes.new: It began in the winter of 1734-35 in Northampton, Massachusetts. There the town's minister, Jonathan Edwards, watched an ordinary church in the Connecticut Valley come apart and remake itself in a wave of conversions. Among them were the poet Phillis Wheatley and the preacher Samson Occom.

prose_changes.old: When an ordinary Massachusetts congregation began converting in waves during the winter of 1734–35, its pastor Jonathan Edwards did something unusual: he wrote down what happened case by case, including a four-year-old girl and a young woman the town had thought beyond hope. The awakening split New England's churches between defenders and critics of the revival, and produced the first substantial body of Christian writing by Black and Native people in the colonies.

The awakening split New England's churches between those who stood up for the revival and those who attacked it. Black and Native Christians of its world also began to write. prose_changes.old: It left no church of its own — the awakening ran through existing Congregational parishes and broke some of them — but it reshaped American religion permanently. It made the revival meeting and the itinerant preacher normal instruments, filled the Baptist churches with Separate converts, and produced in Edwards the most substantial theologian America has yet made, still argued over three centuries later. It seeded the first generation of Black and Native Christian writing in North America. And the missionary societies of the following century traced their impulse back to it, often explicitly, through Edwards's Life of David Brainerd.
prose_changes.new: It left no church of its own. The awakening ran through the old parish churches and broke some of them. But it reshaped American religion for good. It made the revival meeting and the traveling preacher normal tools of church life. The Separate congregations it threw off may have filled many Baptist churches, though that is hard to measure. In Edwards it gave America its most substantial theologian, still argued over three centuries later. Black and Native Christians of its world began to write. And the missionary movement looked back to it. In 1792 William Carey, pleading for a Baptist mission, held up David Brainerd as a model. Edwards had written Brainerd's life from his diary.
prose_changes.reason: Three claims corrected. 'Filled the Baptist churches with Separate converts' is now a stated possibility. 'The missionary societies of the following century traced their impulse back to it, often explicitly' is reduced to the documented case: Carey in 1792 holding up Brainerd. 'Seeded the first generation of Black and Native Christian writing' is reduced to 'began to write'. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept. Round 1: R1-23: build language removed, wording varied.

prose_changes.old: The Baptists grew out of Puritan-Separatist ferment in England. They arrived at Anabaptist-like convictions about believer's baptism largely on their own — historians are divided on how much direct contact there was between the two movements. From the Baptists came William Carey's missionary movement and the Black Baptist churches, which in turn became one of the founding traditions of the Black Church in America.
prose_changes.new: The Baptists grew out of Puritan and Separatist ferment in England. In 1609 John Smyth wrote that his people had moved from Puritanism to Separatism, and then to the baptism of believers. They seem to have reached that belief largely on their own. Historians are divided on how much the Anabaptists shaped it. Soon after, Smyth and his followers asked to join a Mennonite church in Amsterdam. From the Baptists came William Carey's mission and the Black Baptist churches. Those churches in turn became one of the founding traditions of the Black Church in America.
prose_changes.reason: The contact sentence was wrong in shape: contact is documented (Smyth's application to the Waterlander Mennonites), while the dispute is over influence on the 1609 baptism. The two are now separated. Smyth's own 1609 statement of the Puritan-Separatist descent is added. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: In 1609 an exiled English congregation in Amsterdam concluded that baptism belonged to believers who could profess faith for themselves, and its pastor John Smyth baptized himself and then the rest — the beginning of the English Baptists. Two streams developed, General Baptists holding that Christ died for all and Particular Baptists holding to a Calvinist election, and both organized as gathered churches. Bodies of ordinary people who covenanted together, chose their own ministers, disciplined their own members and wrote it all down in minute books, week after week. They were persecuted hard under the Restoration — John Bunyan spent twelve years in Bedford gaol for preaching without a license and wrote Grace Abounding there. And they became one of the strongest voices in English for liberty of conscience. In America they grew explosively out of the awakening, and the movement's outward turn came in 1792, when a Northamptonshire shoemaker named William Carey persuaded a small association of ministers to found a missionary society and then sailed for India himself.
prose_changes.new: In 1609 an exiled English congregation in Amsterdam decided that baptism belonged to believers who could profess faith for themselves. Its pastor, John Smyth, baptized himself and then the rest. That was the start of the English Baptists. Two streams grew up. General Baptists held that Christ died for all. Particular Baptists held, with Calvin, that God had chosen who would be saved. Both formed gathered churches: bodies of ordinary people who made a covenant together and chose their own ministers. They disciplined their own members and wrote it all down in minute books, week after week. They were persecuted hard under the Restoration. John Bunyan spent twelve years in Bedford jail for preaching without a license and wrote Grace Abounding there. They became one of the strongest voices in English for freedom of conscience. In America they grew fast late in the eighteenth century. The awakening may have fed them many converts, though the numbers are not known. The movement turned outward in 1792. That year a shoemaker named William Carey persuaded a small group of ministers to found a mission society. Then he sailed for India himself.
prose_changes.reason: 'In America they grew explosively out of the awakening' has no vendored source for the tie to the awakening (Rippon shows the growth, not its origin); qualified with the reason. Rewritten whole for reading level (it scored below the floor); every other fact kept. 'Gaol' given its American spelling. Round 1: R1-23: build language removed, wording varied.

prose_changes.old: Baptists are now one of the largest Protestant families in the world. The tradition's argument that no magistrate has authority over belief passed into Rhode Island's founding under Roger Williams and, through a long line of Baptist petitioning, into the American constitutional settlement on religion. Carey's society opened the era of Protestant foreign missions and was quickly imitated across the denominations. And the Black Baptist churches founded by Liele, George and their successors became one of the central institutions of African American life, and the ground from which the civil rights movement later grew.
prose_changes.new: Baptists are now one of the largest Protestant families in the world. The tradition held that no ruler has power over what people believe. That idea passed into the founding of Rhode Island under Roger Williams. Through many years of Baptist pleas to the state, it also shaped how the American constitution treats religion. Carey's was not the first Protestant mission. Carey himself named the Danes at Tranquebar and the Moravians before him. But his society sent Carey and John Thomas to India, and Baptist work abroad grew from there. The Black Baptist churches begun by Liele, George and those who came after became a pillar of Black life in America. They were also the ground from which the civil rights movement later grew.
prose_changes.reason: 'Carey's society opened the era of Protestant foreign missions and was quickly imitated across the denominations' is contradicted by Carey's own Enquiry, which names the Danish mission at Tranquebar and the Moravians before him, and the imitation has no vendored source. Rewritten to what the texts show. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: The roughly two thousand ministers ejected from the Church of England in 1662 built a lasting tradition: the dissenting academies, Isaac Watts and the hymn revolution he began, and the 1719 Salters' Hall meeting, after which many Presbyterian congregations drifted toward Arian and then Unitarian belief while the Congregationalists stayed orthodox and were reinvigorated by the eighteenth-century revival. Together with the Quakers and the Baptists, this tradition makes up the wider family of English Dissent.
prose_changes.new: About two thousand ministers were put out of the Church of England in 1662. They built a lasting tradition. It gave England its own schools, the dissenting academies. It also gave Isaac Watts, who changed how English churches sang. In 1719 its ministers met at Salters' Hall in London. After that, many Presbyterian churches drifted away from the Trinity. They moved first toward Arian and then toward Unitarian views. The Congregationalists kept the old faith, and some of their leaders took up the new revival. Watts helped print Jonathan Edwards's story of the awakening in New England. Philip Doddridge asked John Wesley to teach his students. With the Quakers and the Baptists, it makes up the wider family of English Dissent. Baptist ministers sat at Salters' Hall too.
prose_changes.reason: 'Reinvigorated by the eighteenth-century revival' is a broad claim no source in hand makes; Curnock even notes Doddridge was almost the only leading Dissenter friendly to Wesley. Rewritten to the documented contacts (Watts and Edwards's narrative; Doddridge and Wesley) and the Baptist presence at Salters' Hall. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept. Round 1: R1-04: 'took up the new revival' said more than two individuals show; now 'some of their leaders'.

prose_changes.old: On St Bartholomew's Day 1662 about two thousand ministers who could not accept the restored Prayer Book and episcopal ordination were put out of the Church of England, and English Presbyterianism and Congregationalism became permanently separate traditions rather than parties inside one church. Barred from the universities, they built their own: the dissenting academies, which taught mathematics, science and modern languages when Oxford and Cambridge largely did not, and educated a striking share of the country's scientists, manufacturers and reformers. Their other great contribution was sung. dispositions.reason: The Jesuits in the Philippines were one of this church's own parish orders, listed here as members, like the other friars. Membership is not a relationship between two movements.

dispositions.sentence: The century's strains were institutional: a long fight over whether bishops could inspect the friars' parishes, the British occupation of Manila in 1762-64, the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1768, and above all the question of whether Filipino secular priests could hold parishes at all.
dispositions.reason: The Jesuits in the Philippines were one of this church's own parish orders; the 1768 expulsion was a Spanish Crown act carried out on them inside this church, not an act of one movement on another.

dispositions.sentence: By the mid-seventeenth century the Philippines were the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, built parish by parish around Spanish friars who were often the only European in town and the only one who could preach in the local language.
dispositions.reason: Spanish friars: members.

dispositions.sentence: Filipino Christianity found its own voice inside that arrangement in the pasyon, a long verse account of Christ's passion chanted by ordinary people through Holy Week in their own houses — the earliest surviving text dates to 1704 — even as the century's real strain built around whether Filipino priests, and not only Spanish friars, could ever hold parishes of their own.
dispositions.reason: Filipino priests: a group inside this church.

dispositions.sentence: The unresolved question of the period, whether Filipino priests could run Filipino parishes, produced the executions of the three priests remembered as Gomburza in 1872 and fed directly into the national revolution and into the independent Philippine church that broke from Rome in 1902.
dispositions.reason: Gomburza tie carried by the continued-as link (Pardo de Tavera).
